paragraphs.context: everybody said she was the most disagreeable-looking child ever seen
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mary was an unpleasant-looking, selfish child. Her mother did not want her, and the servants did what she said.
paragraphs.simple: When Mary Lennox was sent to Misselthwaite Manor to live with her uncle, everybody said that she was the child with the most unpleasant look they had ever seen. It was true, too. She had a little thin face and a little thin body, thin light hair and a sour look. Her hair was yellow, and her face was yellow, because she had been born in India and had always been ill in one way or another. Her father had had a job under the English Government. He had always been busy and ill himself. Her mother had been a great beauty who cared only to go to parties and have fun with happy people. She had not wanted a little girl at all. When Mary was born, she gave her to an Ayah to look after. The Ayah was made to understand that if she wanted to please the Mem Sahib, she must keep the child out of sight as much as possible. So when Mary was a sick, crying, ugly baby, she was kept out of the way. When she was a sick, crying child just learning to walk, she was kept out of the way too. She never remembered knowing any faces well except the dark faces of her Ayah and the other servants from India. They always did what she said and gave her her own way in everything, because the Mem Sahib would be angry if Mary's crying disturbed her. So by the time she was six years old, she was as selfish and bossy a little pig as ever lived. The young English governess who came to teach her to read and write did not like her, and left after three months. When other governesses came to try to take the job, they always went away in a shorter time than the first one. So if Mary had not chosen to really want to learn to read books, she would never have learned her letters at all.

paragraphs.context: Mary alternately cried and slept through the hours
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mary is alone in the house during the second day of the sickness. She drinks some wine and falls asleep.
paragraphs.simple: During the confusion of the second day, Mary hid in the nursery, and everyone forgot her. Nobody thought of her and nobody wanted her. Strange things happened that she knew nothing about. Mary cried and then slept, and cried and then slept again, through the hours. She only knew that people were ill and that she heard strange and frightening sounds. Once she went quietly into the dining-room and found it empty. But a meal that was only half finished was on the table. The chairs and plates looked as if the people had pushed them back in a hurry when they got up suddenly for some reason. The child ate some fruit and biscuits. She was thirsty, so she drank a glass of wine that stood nearly full. It was sweet, and she did not know how strong it was. Very soon it made her very sleepy. She went back to her nursery and shut herself in again. She was afraid because of the cries she heard in the huts and the sound of feet hurrying. The wine made her so sleepy that she could hardly keep her eyes open. She lay down on her bed and knew nothing more for a long time.

paragraphs.context: She was a stout woman, with very red cheeks and sharp black eyes
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mary goes to England with an officer's wife. Mr Craven's housekeeper, Mrs Medlock, meets her in London.
paragraphs.simple: Mary made the long trip to England by ship, with an officer's wife. The woman was taking her own children to leave them at a boarding-school. She thought only about her own little boy and girl. She was rather glad to give Mary to the woman that Mr. Archibald Craven sent to meet her in London. This woman was his housekeeper at Misselthwaite Manor, and her name was Mrs. Medlock. She was a fat woman, with very red cheeks and sharp black eyes. She wore a very purple dress, a black silk coat with a hanging black fringe on it, and a black bonnet with purple velvet flowers that stuck up and shook when she moved her head. Mary did not like her at all. But Mary very seldom liked people, so there was nothing special in that. Also, it was very clear that Mrs. Medlock did not think much of Mary.

paragraphs.context: it’s a grand big place in a gloomy way
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mrs Medlock tells Mary about Misselthwaite Manor. It is a very big old house at the edge of the moor, with many rooms shut up.
paragraphs.simple: 'It is a big, fine place in a sad and dark way,' Mrs. Medlock said, 'and Mr. Craven is proud of it in his way. And that is sad enough, too. The house is six hundred years old and it is at the edge of the moor. There are nearly a hundred rooms in it, though most of them are shut up and locked. There are pictures and fine old furniture and things that have been there for ages. There is a big park round it, and gardens, and trees with branches hanging down to the ground, some of them.' She stopped and took another breath. 'But there is nothing else,' she ended suddenly.

paragraphs.context: The carriage lamps shed a yellow light on a rough-looking road
paragraphs.mainIdea: The carriage reaches the moor in the dark. Mary hears the wind, which makes a strange sound.
paragraphs.simple: The lamps of the carriage threw a yellow light on a rough-looking road. The road seemed to be cut through bushes and low plants. These ended in a great wide area of dark that seemed to spread out in front of them and all around them. A wind was rising and making a strange, wild, low, rushing sound.

paragraphs.context: The entrance door was a huge one made of massive, curiously shaped panels
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mary enters the great hall of Misselthwaite Manor. It is so dark that she feels small and lost.
paragraphs.simple: The door at the front was a huge one. It was made of heavy, oddly shaped pieces of oak, with big iron nails in them, and it was held together with great iron bars. It opened into an enormous hall. The hall was so dimly lit that the faces in the pictures on the walls, and the figures in the metal suits, made Mary feel she did not want to look at them. She stood on the stone floor and looked like a very small, strange, black figure. She felt as small and lost and strange as she looked.

paragraphs.context: The native servants she had been used to in India
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mary is surprised that Martha talks to her in such a free way. In India servants did not do that.
paragraphs.simple: Mary listened to Martha with a serious, puzzled look. The servants from India that she had been used to were not at all like this. They were too eager to please, and always did what they were told. They did not dare to talk to their masters as if they were equals. They made salaams and called them 'protector of the poor' and names like that. Indian servants were ordered to do things, and not asked. It was not the custom to say 'please' and 'thank you', and Mary had always slapped her Ayah in the face when she was angry. She wondered a little what this girl would do if someone slapped her in the face. Martha was a round, rosy girl who looked good-natured. But she had a strong way about her. It made Mistress Mary wonder if she might even slap back, if the person who hit her was only a little girl.

paragraphs.context: It had not been the custom that Mistress Mary should do anything but stand
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mary begins to see that life at Misselthwaite will teach her new things. Martha is not a trained servant.
paragraphs.simple: It had not been the custom for Mistress Mary to do anything but stand and let herself be dressed like a doll. But before she was ready for breakfast, she began to think that her life at Misselthwaite Manor would end by teaching her a number of new things. These were things like putting on her own shoes and stockings, and picking up things that she dropped. If Martha had been a well-trained maid for a fine young lady, she would have been more ready to obey and be respectful. She would have known that it was her job to brush hair, and button boots, and pick things up and put them away. But Martha was only an untrained country girl from Yorkshire. She had grown up in a cottage on the moor, with a crowd of little brothers and sisters. They had never dreamed of doing anything but looking after themselves and the younger ones, who were babies in arms or just learning to walk.

paragraphs.context: Mrs. Medlock said it’s not to be talked about
paragraphs.mainIdea: Martha tells Mary why Mr Craven hates the garden. It was his wife's garden, and she died after a branch broke.
paragraphs.simple: 'Mind,' she said, 'Mrs. Medlock said we must not talk about it. There are many things in this place that we must not talk about. Those are Mr. Craven's orders. He says his troubles are not the servants' business. But if it were not for the garden, he would not be as he is. It was Mrs. Craven's garden. She made it when they were first married, and she loved it. They used to look after the flowers themselves. None of the gardeners was ever let in. He and she used to go in and shut the door and stay there for hours and hours, reading and talking. She was just a girl, and there was an old tree with a branch bent like a seat. She made roses grow over it, and she used to sit there. But one day, when she was sitting there, the branch broke and she fell to the ground. She was hurt so badly that she died the next day. The doctors thought he would go out of his mind and die too. That is why he hates it. Nobody has gone in since, and he will not let anyone talk about it.'

paragraphs.context: She opened the door of the room and went into the corridor
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mary walks through the corridors and looks at the pictures in the gallery. She feels the faces are looking at her.
paragraphs.simple: Mary opened the door of the room and went into the corridor, and then she began her wanderings. It was a long corridor, and it branched into other corridors. It led her up short flights of steps which went up to others again. There were doors and doors, and there were pictures on the walls. Sometimes they were pictures of dark, strange landscapes, but most often they were portraits of men and women in strange, grand clothes made of satin and velvet. She found herself in one long gallery whose walls were covered with these portraits. She had never thought there could be so many in any house. She walked slowly down this place and stared at the faces, which also seemed to stare at her. She felt as if they were wondering what a little girl from India was doing in their house. Some were pictures of children. There were little girls in thick satin frocks which reached to their feet and stood out about them. There were boys with puffed sleeves and lace collars and long hair, or with big ruffs around their necks. She always stopped to look at the children and to wonder what their names were, and where they had gone, and why they wore such odd clothes. There was a stiff, plain little girl rather like herself. She wore a green brocade dress and held a green parrot on her finger. Her eyes had a sharp, curious look.

paragraphs.context: The rainstorm had ended and the gray mist and clouds had been swept away
paragraphs.mainIdea: The storm is over and the sky is a deep, bright blue. Mary has never seen a sky like it.
paragraphs.simple: The rainstorm had ended. The wind had swept away the gray mist and clouds in the night. The wind itself had stopped, and a bright, deep blue sky curved high over the moorland. Mary had never dreamed of a sky so blue. In India the skies were hot and blazing. This sky was a deep cool blue that almost seemed to sparkle like the water of a lovely lake with no bottom. Here and there, high up in the curved blueness, small clouds of snow-white wool floated. The moor, which went on a long way, looked softly blue. It no longer looked dark purple-black or awful gray.

paragraphs.context: She looked at the key quite a long time
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mary thinks about the key. She would like to open the closed garden and play there alone.
paragraphs.simple: She looked at the key for quite a long time. She turned it over and over and thought about it. As the writer has said before, she was not a child who had been taught to ask permission or ask older people about things. All she thought about the key was this: if it was the key to the closed garden, and she could find where the door was, she could perhaps open it. She could see what was inside the walls and what had happened to the old rose-trees. She wanted to see the garden because it had been shut up for so long. It seemed that it must be different from other places, and that something strange must have happened to it in ten years. Besides, if she liked it, she could go into it every day and shut the door behind her. She could make up some play of her own and play it quite alone. Nobody would know where she was, but would think that the door was still locked and the key buried in the earth. The thought of that pleased her very much.

paragraphs.context: It was the sweetest, most mysterious-looking place anyone could imagine
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mary sees the secret garden. Climbing roses cover the walls and trees. She cannot tell if they are dead or alive.
paragraphs.simple: It was the sweetest, most mysterious-looking place that anyone could imagine. The high walls that shut it in were covered with the bare stems of climbing roses, so thick that they were twisted together. Mary Lennox knew they were roses, because she had seen a great many roses in India. All the ground was covered with grass of a winter brown. Out of it grew groups of bushes which were surely rosebushes, if they were alive. There were many standard roses that had spread their branches so much that they were like little trees. There were other trees in the garden. One of the things that made the place look strangest and loveliest was that climbing roses had run all over these trees. They had swung down long thin curling stems which made light swinging curtains. Here and there the roses had caught hold of each other, or of a branch that reached far, and had crept from one tree to another and made lovely bridges of themselves. There were no leaves and no roses on them now, and Mary did not know if they were dead or alive. But their thin gray or brown branches looked like a kind of misty cloak spreading over everything, walls, trees, and even the brown grass, where they had fallen from their ties and run along the ground. It was this misty tangle from tree to tree that made it all look so mysterious. Mary had thought it must be different from other gardens which had not been left all by themselves for so long. And it was different from any other place she had ever seen in her life.

paragraphs.context: During that week of sunshine, she became more intimate with Ben Weatherstaff
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mary becomes friendlier with Ben Weatherstaff. He does not mind her as much as before, and she is more polite.
paragraphs.simple: During that week of sunshine, Mary became closer to Ben Weatherstaff. She surprised him several times by seeming to start up beside him, as if she had sprung out of the earth. The truth was that she was afraid he would pick up his tools and go away if he saw her coming. So she always walked toward him as quietly as she could. But he did not mind her as strongly as he had at first. Perhaps he was secretly rather pleased that she clearly wanted to be with an old man. Also, she was more polite than she had been. He did not know that when she first saw him, she spoke to him as she would have spoken to a native of India. She had not known that a cross, strong old Yorkshire man was not used to bowing to his masters and just being ordered by them to do things.

paragraphs.context: It was a very strange thing indeed
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mary sees Dickon for the first time. He plays a pipe, and wild animals come near to listen.
paragraphs.simple: It was a very strange thing. She stopped to look at it, and for a moment she could hardly breathe. A boy was sitting under a tree with his back against it, playing on a rough wooden pipe. He was a funny-looking boy of about twelve. He looked very clean. His nose turned up and his cheeks were as red as poppies. Mistress Mary had never seen such round and such blue eyes in any boy's face. On the trunk of the tree he leaned against, a brown squirrel was holding on and watching him. From behind a bush nearby, a male pheasant was carefully stretching his neck to peep out. Quite near him were two rabbits sitting up and sniffing with shaking noses. It really seemed as if they were all coming nearer to watch him and listen to the strange low little call that his pipe made.

paragraphs.context: I never ketched cold since I was born
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dickon says he never catches cold because he has always been out in all kinds of weather.
paragraphs.simple: 'Not me,' he said, with a grin. 'I have never caught a cold since I was born. I was not brought up weak. I have run about on the moor in all weathers, like the rabbits do. Mother says I have sniffed in too much fresh air for twelve years to ever start sniffing because of a cold. I am as tough as a stick from a hawthorn tree.'

paragraphs.context: Mrs. Medlock says it’s because o’ mother
paragraphs.mainIdea: Martha tells why Mr Craven wants to see Mary. Martha's mother stopped him on the road and spoke about Mary.
paragraphs.simple: 'Well,' explained Martha, 'Mrs. Medlock says it is because of mother. Mother was walking to Thwaite village and she met him. She had never spoken to him before, but Mrs. Craven had been to our cottage two or three times. He had forgotten, but mother had not, and she dared to stop him. I do not know what she said to him about you, but she said something that put it in his mind to see you before he goes away again tomorrow.'

paragraphs.context: The door of her room was ajar and the sound came down the corridor
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mary hears crying again at night. She decides to find out what it is.
paragraphs.simple: The door of her room was a little open, and the sound came down the corridor. It was a far-off faint sound of unhappy crying. She listened for a few minutes, and each minute she became more and more sure. She felt that she must find out what it was. It seemed even stranger than the secret garden and the buried key. Perhaps she was in a mood to break rules, and this made her brave. She put her foot out of bed and stood on the floor.

paragraphs.context: He lay quite still and listened while she went on talking
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mary tells Colin about the garden, the robin and Ben Weatherstaff. The talk about the robin makes Colin smile.
paragraphs.simple: He lay quite still and listened while she went on talking. She spoke about the roses, which might have climbed from tree to tree and hung down. She spoke about the many birds which might have built their nests there because it was so safe. Then she told him about the robin and Ben Weatherstaff. There was so much to tell about the robin, and it was so easy and safe to talk about it, that she stopped feeling afraid. The robin pleased him so much that he smiled until he looked almost beautiful. At first Mary had thought that he was even plainer than herself, with his big eyes and heavy locks of hair.

paragraphs.context: Nobody knows for sure and certain
paragraphs.mainIdea: Martha tells Mary what is wrong with Colin. Mr Craven went out of his mind when Colin was born because Mrs Craven died.
paragraphs.simple: 'Nobody knows for sure and certain,' said Martha. 'Mr. Craven went out of his mind when the baby was born. The doctors thought he would have to be put in an asylum. It was because Mrs. Craven died, like I told you. He would not set eyes on the baby. He just raved and said it would be another hunchback like him, and it had better die.'

paragraphs.context: It was the best thing she could have said
paragraphs.mainIdea: Talking about Dickon and the moor makes Mary and Colin laugh like two ordinary healthy children.
paragraphs.simple: It was the best thing she could have said. To talk about Dickon meant to talk about the moor and the cottage, and the fourteen people who lived in it on sixteen shillings a week. It meant the children who got fat on the moor grass like the wild ponies. It meant Dickon's mother and the skipping-rope, and the moor with the sun on it, and the pale green points sticking up out of the black earth. It was all so alive that Mary talked more than she had ever talked before, and Colin both talked and listened as he had never done either before. They began to laugh over nothing, as children do when they are happy together. In the end they were making as much noise as two ordinary, healthy, natural ten-year-old children, instead of a hard, little, unloving girl and a sickly boy who believed that he was going to die.

paragraphs.context: In her talks with Colin, Mary had tried to be very cautious
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mary is careful about the secret garden when she talks with Colin. She wants to know if he can keep a secret and if she could take him there without anyone knowing.
paragraphs.simple: In her talks with Colin, Mary had tried to be very careful about the secret garden. There were certain things she wanted to find out from him, but she felt that she must find them out without asking him direct questions. First, as she began to like being with him, she wanted to know if he was the kind of boy you could tell a secret to. He was not at all like Dickon, but he was so pleased with the idea of a garden no one knew about that she thought he could perhaps be trusted. But she had not known him long enough to be sure. The second thing she wanted to find out was this. If he could be trusted, would it be possible to take him to the garden without anyone finding out? The grand doctor had said that he must have fresh air, and Colin had said that he would not mind fresh air in a secret garden. Perhaps if he had a great deal of fresh air, and knew Dickon and the robin, and saw things growing, he might not think so much about dying. Mary had seen herself in the glass sometimes lately. She had seen that she looked quite different from the child she had seen when she arrived from India. This child looked nicer. Even Martha had seen a change in her.

paragraphs.context: Everybody as knowed about Mester Craven knowed there was a little lad
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dickon explains how he knew about Colin. People who knew Mr Craven knew about the boy, and Mrs Medlock talks about him at the Sowerby cottage.
paragraphs.simple: 'Everybody who knew about Mr. Craven knew there was a little boy who was likely to be a cripple. They knew Mr. Craven did not like him to be talked about. People are sorry for Mr. Craven because Mrs. Craven was such a pretty young lady, and they were so fond of each other. Mrs. Medlock stops in our cottage whenever she goes to Thwaite. She does not mind talking to mother in front of us children, because she knows we have been brought up to be trusty. How did you find out about him? Martha was in a lot of trouble the last time she came home. She said you had heard him crying and you were asking questions, and she did not know what to say.'

paragraphs.context: She was no more used to considering other people than Colin was
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mary is not used to thinking about other people, just like Colin. She sees no reason why a bad-tempered boy should stop her doing what she likes best.
paragraphs.simple: Mary pressed her lips tightly together. She was no more used to thinking about other people than Colin was. She saw no reason why a bad-tempered boy should get in the way of the thing she liked best. She knew nothing about how sad it is for people who have been ill and nervous, and who do not know that they can control their tempers. They need not make other people ill and nervous too. When she had had a headache in India, she had done her best to see that everybody else also had a headache, or something as bad. She felt she was quite right. But now she felt that Colin was quite wrong.

paragraphs.context: No one but Colin himself knew what effect those crossly spoken childish words
paragraphs.mainIdea: Colin had never talked about his secret fears. Now Mary says he is not as ill as he thinks, and he starts to feel she may be right.
paragraphs.simple: No one but Colin himself knew what effect those angry childish words had on him. If he had ever had anyone to talk to about his secret terrors, and if he had ever dared to ask questions, he would have found out that most of his fright and illness was made by himself. If he had had childish companions, and had not lain on his back in the huge closed house, breathing an atmosphere heavy with the fears of people who were mostly ignorant and tired of him, he would have found this out. But he had lain and thought of himself and his aches and tiredness for hours and days and months and years. Now an angry little girl, with no sympathy, said firmly that he was not as ill as he thought. He actually felt as if she might be telling the truth.

paragraphs.context: Aye, that we mun,” she said (which meant
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mary tries to speak Yorkshire to Dickon and tells him what they will do first. Dickon is amused.
paragraphs.simple: 'Aye, that we mun,' she said, which meant 'Yes, indeed, we must.' 'I will tell you what we will do first,' she went on. Dickon grinned, because it amused him very much when the little girl tried to twist her tongue to speak Yorkshire. 'He has taken a great fancy to you. He wants to see you and he wants to see Soot and Captain. When I go back to the house to talk to him, I will ask him if you cannot come and see him tomorrow morning, and bring your creatures with you. Then in a little while, when there are more leaves out, and perhaps a bud or two, we will get him to come out. You will push him in his chair and we will bring him here and show him everything.'

paragraphs.context: Well, sir,” answered Mrs. Medlock, “you’ll scarcely believe your eyes
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mrs Medlock tells Dr Craven that Mary has changed Colin. Mary stood up to him last night and made him stop screaming.
paragraphs.simple: 'Well, sir,' answered Mrs. Medlock, 'you will hardly believe your eyes when you see him. That plain sour-faced child, who is almost as bad as he is, has just put a spell on him. There is no telling how she did it. The Lord knows she is nothing to look at, and you hardly ever hear her speak. But she did what none of us dare to do. She flew at him like a little cat last night, and stamped her feet and ordered him to stop screaming. Somehow she startled him so much that he did stop. And this afternoon, well, just come up and see, sir. It is hard to believe.'

paragraphs.context: And then she paused for breath
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dickon found a newborn lamb on the moor three days ago. He fed it with warm milk, and Mary held it on her lap.
paragraphs.simple: And then she stopped for breath. Dickon had found the newborn lamb three days before, lying by its dead mother among the gorse bushes on the moor. It was not the first lamb without a mother that he had found, and he knew what to do with it. He had taken it to the cottage wrapped in his jacket, and had let it lie near the fire and had fed it with warm milk. It was a soft thing with a darling silly baby face and legs rather long for its body. Dickon had carried it over the moor in his arms, and its feeding bottle was in his pocket with a squirrel. When Mary had sat under a tree with its limp warmth in her lap, she had felt too full of strange joy to speak. A lamb, a lamb! A living lamb who lay on your lap like a baby!

paragraphs.context: It was perhaps well he had been prepared or he might have been startled
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mr Roach goes into Colin's room. A crow on a chair says 'Caw' and he almost jumps back.
paragraphs.simple: It was perhaps good that he had been told what to expect, or he might have been startled. When the bedroom door was opened, a large crow sat on the high back of a carved chair. It seemed quite at home there. It said 'Caw, Caw' quite loudly to tell that a visitor had come in. In spite of Mrs. Medlock's warning, Mr. Roach only just stopped himself from jumping backward, which would have been very undignified.

paragraphs.context: But Colin had actually dropped back against his cushions
paragraphs.mainIdea: Colin covers his eyes until the chair is inside the garden. Then he looks around and sees the green leaves, the flowers and the sun.
paragraphs.simple: But Colin had actually dropped back against his cushions, even though he gasped with delight. He had covered his eyes with his hands and held them there, shutting out everything, until they were inside and the chair stopped as if by magic and the door was closed. Not until then did he take them away and look round and round and round, as Dickon and Mary had done. Over walls and earth and trees and swinging sprays and tendrils the fair green veil of tender little leaves had crept. In the grass under the trees and the gray urns in the alcoves, and here and there everywhere, were touches or splashes of gold and purple and white. The trees were showing pink and snow above his head. There were fluttering of wings and faint sweet pipes and humming and scents and scents. The sun fell warm upon his face like a hand with a lovely touch. In wonder Mary and Dickon stood and stared at him. He looked so strange and different because a pink glow of color had actually crept all over him, ivory face and neck and hands and all.

paragraphs.context: One of the strange things about living in the world
paragraphs.mainIdea: The author says that now and then a person feels sure that he will live for ever. This can happen at dawn, at sunset, at night or in someone's eyes.
paragraphs.simple: One of the strange things about living in the world is that only now and then is one quite sure one is going to live for ever and ever. One knows it sometimes when one gets up at the soft, serious time of dawn and goes out and stands alone. One throws one's head far back and looks up and up, and watches the pale sky slowly changing and flushing, and wonderful unknown things happening, until the East almost makes one cry out, and one's heart stands still at the strange unchanging greatness of the rising of the sun. It has been happening every morning for thousands and thousands and thousands of years. One knows it then for a moment or so. One knows it sometimes when one stands by oneself in a wood at sunset, and the mysterious deep gold stillness coming through and under the branches seems to be saying something slowly, again and again, that one cannot quite hear, however much one tries. Then sometimes the great quiet of the dark blue at night, with millions of stars waiting and watching, makes one sure. Sometimes a sound of far-off music makes it true, and sometimes a look in someone's eyes.

paragraphs.context: It was too much. The strength which Colin usually threw into his tantrums
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ben asks if Colin has crooked legs. Colin is so angry that he finds a new strength.
paragraphs.simple: It was too much. The strength which Colin usually threw into his tantrums rushed through him now in a new way. Never yet had he been accused of crooked legs, even in whispers. Ben Weatherstaff's voice showed that he simply believed they were crooked, and this was more than a Rajah's flesh and blood could stand. His anger and hurt pride made him forget everything but this one moment. They filled him with a power he had never known before, an almost unnatural strength.

paragraphs.context: She was so fond of it —she was!” said Ben Weatherstaff slowly
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ben says Mrs Craven asked him to take care of her roses if she was ill or went away. He climbed over the wall once a year until his rheumatism stopped him.
paragraphs.simple: 'She was so fond of it, she was!' said Ben Weatherstaff slowly. 'And she was such a pretty young thing. She said to me once, laughing, "Ben, if ever I am ill or if I go away, you must take care of my roses." When she did go away, the orders were that no one was ever to come near. But I came,' he said, with grumpy stubbornness. 'I came over the wall, until the rheumatism stopped me, and I did a bit of work once a year. She had given her order first.'

paragraphs.context: The great scientific discoveries I am going to make
paragraphs.mainIdea: Colin says his discoveries will be about Magic. He says there is Magic in everything and people do not yet know how to use it.
paragraphs.simple: 'The great scientific discoveries I am going to make,' he went on, 'will be about Magic. Magic is a great thing, and hardly anyone knows anything about it except a few people in old books, and Mary a little, because she was born in India where there are fakirs. I believe Dickon knows some Magic, but perhaps he does not know he knows it. He charms animals and people. I would never have let him come to see me if he had not been an animal charmer, which is a boy charmer too, because a boy is an animal. I am sure there is Magic in everything, only we have not sense enough to get hold of it and make it do things for us, like electricity and horses and steam.'

paragraphs.context: He does it to keep them from guessin’ what’s happened
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dickon explains that Colin still complains so that no one guesses what has happened. Colin wants to show his father that he is as straight as other boys.
paragraphs.simple: 'He does it to keep them from guessing what has happened. If the doctor knew he had found out he could stand on his feet, he would likely write and tell Mr. Craven. Master Colin is saving the secret to tell himself. He is going to practise his Magic on his legs every day till his father comes back. Then he is going to march into his room and show him he is as straight as other boys. But he and Miss Mary think it is best to do a bit of groaning and fretting now and then to throw people off the scent.'

paragraphs.context: And the secret garden bloomed and bloomed
paragraphs.mainIdea: The robin's mate sits on eggs in the nest. The robin and his mate feel that everything in the garden understands how precious eggs are.
paragraphs.simple: And the secret garden bloomed and bloomed, and every morning showed new wonders. In the robin's nest there were eggs, and the robin's mate sat upon them, keeping them warm with her feathery little breast and careful wings. At first she was very nervous, and the robin himself watched angrily. Even Dickon did not go near the close-grown corner in those days. He waited until, by some quiet mysterious spell, he seemed to have made the little pair understand that in the garden there was nothing which was not quite like themselves. Nothing there failed to understand the wonderfulness of what was happening to them, the great, tender, terrible, heartbreaking beauty and seriousness of Eggs. If there had been one person in that garden who had not known, deep inside, that if an Egg were taken away or hurt the whole world would whirl round and crash through space and come to an end, and if there had been even one who did not feel it and act as it demanded, there could have been no happiness even in that golden springtime air. But they all knew it and felt it, and the robin and his mate knew they knew it.

paragraphs.context: But at the outset it seemed necessary to be on guard
paragraphs.mainIdea: The robin is afraid of Mary and Colin at first. He sees Colin move in a strange slow way and thinks he may be getting ready to pounce, like a cat.
paragraphs.simple: But at the start it seemed necessary to be on guard against the other two. First, the boy creature did not come into the garden on his legs. He was pushed in on a thing with wheels, and the skins of wild animals were thrown over him. That in itself was doubtful. Then when he began to stand up and move about, he did it in a strange way that was new to him, and the others seemed to have to help him. The robin used to hide himself in a bush and watch this anxiously, his head tilted first on one side and then on the other. He thought that the slow movements might mean that the boy was getting ready to pounce, as cats do. When cats are getting ready to pounce they creep over the ground very slowly. The robin talked this over with his mate a great deal for a few days. After that he decided not to speak of it, because her fear was so great that he was afraid it might hurt the Eggs.

paragraphs.context: That I do, lad,” she answered
paragraphs.mainIdea: Susan Sowerby tells Colin that she does believe in Magic, though she never knew it by that name. She says the same Good Thing that makes seeds swell and the sun shine made him well.
paragraphs.simple: 'That I do, lad,' she answered. 'I never knew it by that name, but what does the name matter? I am sure they call it a different name in France and a different one in Germany. The same thing that made the seeds swell and the sun shine made you a well lad, and it is the Good Thing. It is not like us poor fools who think it matters if we are called out of our names. The Big Good Thing does not stop to worry, bless you. It goes on making worlds by the million, worlds like us. Never you stop believing in the Big Good Thing and knowing the world is full of it. Call it what you like. You were singing to it when I came into the garden.'

paragraphs.context: In each century since the beginning of the world wonderful things have been discovered
paragraphs.mainIdea: The author says that people at first refuse to believe new things, and later they happen. One new thing is that thoughts are as powerful as electric batteries and can be as good as sunlight or as bad as poison.
paragraphs.simple: In each century since the beginning of the world, wonderful things have been found. In the last century more amazing things were found out than in any century before. In this new century hundreds of things that are still more surprising will be brought to light. At first people refuse to believe that a strange new thing can be done. Then they begin to hope it can be done. Then they see it can be done. Then it is done, and all the world wonders why it was not done centuries ago. One of the new things people began to find out in the last century was that thoughts, just mere thoughts, are as powerful as electric batteries. They are as good for one as sunlight is, or as bad for one as poison. To let a sad thought or a bad one get into your mind is as dangerous as letting a scarlet fever germ get into your body. If you let it stay there after it has got in, you may never get over it as long as you live.

paragraphs.context: As he sat gazing into the clear running of the water
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mr Craven sits by a stream in the valley and looks at blue forget-me-nots. His mind and body become quiet, and something seems to be freed in him.
paragraphs.simple: As he sat looking into the clear running of the water, Archibald Craven slowly felt his mind and body both grow quiet, as quiet as the valley itself. He wondered if he were going to sleep, but he was not. He sat and looked at the sunlit water, and his eyes began to see things growing at its edge. There was one lovely mass of blue forget-me-nots growing so close to the stream that its leaves were wet. He found himself looking at these, as he remembered he had looked at such things years ago. He was thinking tenderly how lovely it was and what wonders of blue its hundreds of little blossoms were. He did not know that just that simple thought was slowly filling his mind, filling and filling it until other things were softly pushed aside. It was as if a sweet clear spring had begun to rise in a still, dirty pool, and had risen and risen until at last it swept the dark water away. But of course he did not think of this himself. He only knew that the valley seemed to grow quieter and quieter as he sat and stared at the bright delicate blueness. He did not know how long he sat there or what was happening to him. At last he moved as if he were waking up, and he got up slowly and stood on the moss carpet, drawing a long, deep, soft breath and wondering at himself. Something seemed to have been untied and set free in him, very quietly.

paragraphs.context: And then the dream ended. But he did not awaken.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The dream ends, and Mr Craven sleeps until morning. An Italian servant brings him letters, and he remembers the dream.
paragraphs.simple: And then the dream ended. But he did not wake. He slept soundly and sweetly all through the lovely night. When he did wake at last, it was bright morning and a servant was standing staring at him. He was an Italian servant. He was used, as all the servants of the villa were, to accepting without question any strange thing his foreign master might do. No one ever knew when he would go out or come in, or where he would choose to sleep, or if he would roam about the garden or lie in the boat on the lake all night. The man held a tray with some letters on it, and he waited quietly until Mr. Craven took them. When he had gone away, Mr. Craven sat a few moments holding them in his hand and looking at the lake. His strange calm was still upon him, and something more. It was a lightness, as if the cruel thing which had been done had not happened as he thought, as if something had changed. He was remembering the dream, the real, real dream.

sentences.context: You ought to have gone to the hills two weeks ago
sentences.simple: You should have gone to the hills two weeks ago, but you did not.
sentences.grammar: 'ought to have + past participle' says what was the right thing to do in the past, but it was not done.

sentences.context: who was made to understand that if she wished to please the Mem Sahib
sentences.simple: Someone told the Ayah clearly that if she wanted to please the Mem Sahib, she must keep the child out of sight.
sentences.grammar: 'was made to understand' is a passive form: someone made her know it; 'if she wished ... she must' gives the rule the Ayah had to follow.

sentences.context: What you’re to be kept at Misselthwaite Manor for I don’t know
sentences.simple: I do not know why they are keeping you at Misselthwaite Manor.
sentences.grammar: The word order is not the usual one: 'what ... for' means 'why', and the sentence means 'I don't know why you are to be kept at Misselthwaite Manor'; 'are to be kept' tells what is planned.

sentences.context: If the pretty wife had been alive she might have made things cheerful
sentences.simple: If the pretty wife had been alive, she could perhaps have made things happier.
sentences.grammar: 'If + had been, might have + past participle' is about the past: the wife was not alive, so it did not happen.

sentences.context: it seemed quite proper that other people should wait on one
sentences.simple: It seemed right to Mary that other people should serve her.
sentences.grammar: 'should' here means it is the right thing to do; 'one' means 'a person like her'; 'wait on' means 'serve'.

sentences.context: the trees (which nearly met overhead) made it seem as if they were driving
sentences.simple: The trees nearly touched each other above them, and it seemed as if they were driving through a long dark room.
sentences.grammar: '(which nearly met overhead)' is a side comment about the trees; 'made it seem as if ...' means 'gave the feeling that ...'.

sentences.context: it’s time tha’ should learn. Tha’ cannot begin younger
sentences.simple: It is time that you learned. You cannot begin at a younger age.
sentences.grammar: 'It's time (that) + subject + should + verb' means it is the right time to do something now; 'tha'' is Yorkshire for 'you'.

sentences.context: I can’t abide to see good victuals go to waste
sentences.simple: I cannot stand to see good food wasted.
sentences.grammar: 'can't abide' means 'cannot bear'; 'see + noun + go to waste' is a pattern: see something happen. Martha uses 'victuals', an old word for food.

sentences.context: It must mean that hollow shuddering sort of roar
sentences.simple: Mary thought it must mean the low, shaking, roaring sound that went round and round the house.
sentences.grammar: 'must mean' shows that Mary is almost sure; 'that hollow shuddering sort of roar' is the thing she thinks the word means.

sentences.context: But for th’ garden he wouldn’t be like he is
sentences.simple: If it were not for the garden, he would not be as he is.
sentences.grammar: 'But for + noun' means 'if it were not for'; the result uses 'wouldn't be'. 'th'' is Yorkshire for 'the'.

sentences.context: Since so many rooms had been built, people must have lived in them
sentences.simple: Because so many rooms were built, people must have lived in them.
sentences.grammar: 'must have + past participle' is a guess about the past; 'Since' here means 'because'.

sentences.context: It was not until she climbed to the second floor that she thought
sentences.simple: Only after she climbed to the second floor did she think of turning the handle of a door.
sentences.grammar: 'It was not until ... that ...' puts the focus on the time: the thing happened only then, and not before.

sentences.context: Tha’s never used tha’ legs since tha’ was born, it seems to me
sentences.simple: It seems to me that you have never used your legs since you were born.
sentences.grammar: 'Tha's never used' is Yorkshire for 'You have never used'; 'it seems to me' is an extra comment placed at the end.

sentences.context: He knows every cabbage stump in th’ gardens, let alone th’ people
sentences.simple: He knows every cabbage stump in the gardens, and he knows the people even better.
sentences.grammar: 'let alone' adds a second thing that is even more sure than the first: if he knows the cabbage stumps, he surely knows the people.

sentences.context: Living as it were, all by herself in a house with a hundred
sentences.simple: Living, so to speak, all alone in a house with a hundred rooms that were closed in a mysterious way, had set her mind to work.
sentences.grammar: 'Living ... had set her ... to working' has an -ing phrase as its subject; 'as it were' means 'so to speak'.

sentences.context: If tha’d been our ’Lizabeth Ellen tha’d have give me a kiss
sentences.simple: If you had been our Lizabeth Ellen, you would have given me a kiss.
sentences.grammar: 'If + had been, would have + past participle' is about the past and what did not happen; Martha's Yorkshire says 'give' for 'given'.

sentences.context: If she had been Ben Weatherstaff she could have told
sentences.simple: If Mary had been Ben Weatherstaff, she could have told by looking whether the wood was alive.
sentences.grammar: 'If she had been ... she could have told' is about the past and what did not happen: Mary was not Ben; the next words in the book, 'by looking at it', tell how she could tell.

sentences.context: A woman as brings up twelve children learns something besides her A.B.C.
sentences.simple: A woman who raises twelve children learns something besides her letters.
sentences.grammar: 'as' here is Yorkshire for 'who' in a relative clause; 'brings up' means raises; 'besides' means 'in addition to'.

sentences.context: he would not have stirred for the world, lest his robin should start away
sentences.simple: He did not move at all, because he was afraid his robin would fly away.
sentences.grammar: 'lest ... should' means 'in case' or 'for fear that'; it is an old way to say what you want to avoid.

sentences.context: Birds is rare choosers an’ a robin can flout a body
sentences.simple: Birds are very careful about who they choose, and a robin can treat a person with more disrespect than a man can.
sentences.grammar: 'Birds is' is Yorkshire for 'Birds are'; 'a body' means 'a person'; 'rare choosers' means birds that choose with great care.

sentences.context: I’ve sniffed up too much fresh air for twelve year’
sentences.simple: I have breathed in so much fresh air for twelve years that I will never sniff because of a cold.
sentences.grammar: 'too much ... to ever get to ...' means the amount is so big that the result cannot happen; 'twelve year'' is Yorkshire for 'twelve years'.

sentences.context: Whatever happens, you —you never would tell?
sentences.simple: Whatever happens, you would never tell anyone, would you?
sentences.grammar: 'Whatever happens' means 'no matter what happens'; 'you never would tell?' is a question made from a statement, and 'would' is about what he is willing to do.

sentences.context: I thought her rather bold to stop me on the moor
sentences.simple: I thought she was rather bold, or forward, to stop me on the moor.
sentences.grammar: 'I thought her rather bold' is 'thought + object + adjective' (I had the opinion that she was bold); 'to stop me' tells in what way she was bold.

sentences.context: If I were to live, this place would sometime belong to me
sentences.simple: If I lived, this place would one day be mine.
sentences.grammar: 'If I were to live' is an imagined case about the future; 'would' shows the result.

sentences.context: If she had lived I believe I should not have been ill always
sentences.simple: I believe that if my mother had lived, I would not have been ill all the time.
sentences.grammar: 'If she had lived ... should not have been' is about the past and what did not happen; 'ill always' puts 'always' after the word.

sentences.context: He knows us daren’t call our souls our own
sentences.simple: He knows we do not dare to say that anything is ours.
sentences.grammar: 'us' is Yorkshire for 'we'; 'daren't' is 'dare not'; 'call our souls our own' is a saying: the servants have no freedom.

sentences.context: Have you to do what I please or have you not?
sentences.simple: Do you have to do what I want, or do you not?
sentences.grammar: 'Have you to do' is an old way of asking 'Do you have to do'; 'or have you not' ends the question.

sentences.context: Tha’ knew how to build tha’ nest before tha’ came out o’ th’ egg
sentences.simple: You knew how to build your nest before you came out of the egg.
sentences.grammar: 'Tha'' is Yorkshire for 'you' and 'tha' nest' for 'your nest'; 'knew how to build' is 'knew' plus 'how' plus 'to' and a verb.

sentences.context: way o’ thinkin’ and doin’ things an’ a body had better not meddle
sentences.simple: They have their own way of thinking and doing things, and a person had better not mix in.
sentences.grammar: 'had better not meddle' means 'should not meddle'; 'a body' means 'a person'.

sentences.context: It’s the best thing that could happen to the sickly pampered thing
sentences.simple: It is the best thing that could happen to the weak, spoiled boy.
sentences.grammar: 'the best thing that could happen' uses 'could' for what is possible; 'sickly pampered thing' puts two describing words before 'thing'.

sentences.context: If he had ever had anyone to talk to about his secret terrors
sentences.simple: If he had ever had anyone to talk to about his secret fears.
sentences.grammar: This 'if' clause starts a long sentence about the past that did not happen; 'had had' is 'had' in the past perfect, and the result comes later with 'he would have found out'.

sentences.context: He’s been spoiled till salt won’t save him
sentences.simple: He has been spoiled so much that not even salt can save him.
sentences.grammar: 'He's been spoiled' is the present perfect passive; 'till salt won't save him' is a saying that compares him to spoiled meat which even salt cannot save.

sentences.context: it is not to be wondered at that his doctor felt somewhat startled
sentences.simple: It is no surprise that his doctor felt a little startled.
sentences.grammar: 'it is not to be wondered at that ...' is a formal way to say 'it is not strange that'; 'that' starts the reason.

sentences.context: I’d rather give up the case this moment, sir, than even stay here
sentences.simple: I would rather stop working on this case right now than even stay here.
sentences.grammar: 'would rather ... than' shows a choice; 'give up the case' means stop caring for the patient.

sentences.context: If I wasn’t a bachelder, an’ tha’ was a wench o’ mine
sentences.simple: If I were not a bachelor, and you were a girl of mine.
sentences.grammar: 'If I wasn't ... and you were' starts an imagined case that is finished in the next words; 'bachelder' is Ben's way to say 'bachelor'.

sentences.context: Layin’ tha’ badness on a robin —not but what he’s impidint enow
sentences.simple: You put the blame for your badness on a robin, though he is rude enough for anything.
sentences.grammar: 'Layin'' (laying) starts the phrase without 'You are'; 'not but what' means 'though'.

sentences.context: Th’ world’s full o’ jackasses brayin’ an’ they never bray nowt but lies
sentences.simple: The world is full of fools who bray like donkeys, and all they ever say is lies.
sentences.grammar: 'jackasses brayin'' joins a noun and an '-ing' word to say what they are doing; 'never ... nowt' is a double 'no' in Yorkshire, but the meaning is only 'nothing'.

sentences.context: If you had been his own boy and he had been a slapping sort
sentences.simple: If you had been his own son, and he had been a man who slaps.
sentences.grammar: Both parts use 'if ... had been' for what did not happen; the result comes next, 'he would have slapped you'.

sentences.context: Anything’ll grow for him. His ’taters and cabbages is twice th’ size
sentences.simple: Anything will grow for him. His potatoes and cabbages are twice the size of other people's.
sentences.grammar: 'Anything'll' is 'Anything will'; 'is' for 'are' and ''taters' for 'potatoes' are Yorkshire speech.

sentences.context: If there had been one person in that garden who had not known
sentences.simple: If there had been even one person in that garden who had not known.
sentences.grammar: 'If there had been ... who had not known' is about the past and what did not happen; 'who had not known' tells about the person.

sentences.context: is that a chap can get up an’ say aught he pleases
sentences.simple: The best thing about giving talks is that a man can get up and say anything he likes.
sentences.grammar: 'is that' starts a clause that tells what the best thing is; 'aught' is an old word for 'anything'; 'a chap' is a man.

sentences.context: At first people refuse to believe that a strange new thing can be done
sentences.simple: At first people will not believe that a strange new thing can be done.
sentences.grammar: 'At first ... then ... then' puts the steps in order; 'that a strange new thing can be done' is a passive clause that tells what they refuse to believe.

sentences.context: Of course this was the wrong Magic —to begin by saying “too late.”
sentences.simple: Of course this was the wrong Magic, to begin by saying 'too late'.
sentences.grammar: The words after the dash explain what 'the wrong Magic' was; 'to begin by saying' is 'to begin' plus 'by' and an '-ing' verb.
